lead: When the population standard deviation σ is unknown and the sample is small, we replace σ by the sample standard deviation s. That extra estimation makes the standardized mean more variable, so it follows Student's t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom. The t-test uses this curve to judge a claim about a mean: packet weights, two drug batches, before-after studies such as a new UPI flow and payment time.
prereq: You need the t distribution and confidence intervals from Unit 5, and H₀, critical region and p-value from Chapter 6.1.

blocks.text: The z-test divides the gap between sample mean and claimed mean by σ/√n. In small studies σ is unknown, so we use s from the same data. The denominator is then an estimate and varies from sample to sample.

With small n, s can come out too small, and dividing by a small number inflates the ratio. To keep the false-alarm rate at α, critical values move outwards. Student's t curve has heavier tails and larger critical values than the normal curve.

blocks.where: x̄ is the sample mean; μ₀ is the mean claimed by H₀; s is the sample standard deviation with divisor n − 1; n is the sample size; df is the degrees of freedom of the t curve used for the critical value.

blocks.text: One piece of information is spent on x̄, so only n − 1 deviations can vary freely. As n grows, t approaches the standard normal; beyond about n = 30 the two tables give almost the same critical values, which is why the z-test of Chapter 6.2 is safe for large samples.
The word t-test covers three designs. Choose the formula from the design, not from the size of the numbers.
One sample. Compare the mean of one sample with a claimed value μ₀. One number per unit, df = n − 1.

Two independent samples. Two separate groups, such as two machines, with no pairing between units. Assume both populations are normal with the same variance. Pool the two sample variances, then compare the two means.

blocks.where: s_p² is the pooled variance; s₁² and s₂² are the sample variances of group 1 and group 2; n₁ and n₂ are the sample sizes; n₁ + n₂ − 2 is the total degrees of freedom.
x̄₁ and x̄₂ are the two sample means; s_p is the pooled standard deviation, the square root of s_p²; the denominator is the standard error of the difference of means.

blocks.text: Paired data. The same unit is measured twice, before and after. Reduce each pair to one number d, the difference, and run a one-sample t-test on the differences with μ₀ = 0.

blocks.where: d̄ is the mean of the n differences; s_d is the standard deviation of the differences; n is the number of pairs.

head: Design
df
Typical use
rows: Before and after on same unit

items: Write H₀ and H₁ and fix α. One-tailed or two-tailed decides which column of the t table you read.
Compute x̄ and s (d̄ and s_d for paired data).
Compute the standard error: s/√n for one sample, s_p√(1/n₁ + 1/n₂) for two, s_d/√n for paired.
Compute t and its degrees of freedom.
Read t(α, df) for one-tailed, t(α/2, df) for two-tailed.
Reject H₀ when t falls in the tail named by H₁: t > t(α, df) for H₁: μ > μ₀, t < −t(α, df) for H₁: μ < μ₀. Only for two-tailed do you reject when |t| > t(α/2, df).
State the conclusion in the units of the problem.

blocks.text: The same numbers give a confidence interval. Replace 1.96 by the t critical value.

blocks.where: t(α/2, n−1) is the two-tailed critical value with n − 1 degrees of freedom; the half-width t × s/√n is the margin of error in the units of the data.

items: Observations must be independent. Ten readings in one minute from one machine are not independent.
The population should be roughly normal; with large n the central limit theorem rescues you.
The pooled two-sample form needs equal population variances. Check with the F-test of Chapter 6.4.
When variances clearly differ, Welch's t-test is used; only a few universities teach it in the first course.

examples.question: A random sample of 10 biscuit packets has mean weight 248 g and sample standard deviation 6 g. The label claims 250 g. Test at α = 0.05 whether the true mean is less than 250 g, using t(0.05, 9) = 1.833. Also give a 95% confidence interval, using t(0.025, 9) = 2.262.
steps: H₀: μ = 250 g. H₁: μ < 250 g, left tail. α = 0.05, n = 10, df = 9.
Critical value t(0.05, 9) = 1.833; reject when t < −1.833.
−1.0541 > −1.833, so not in the rejection region.
Fail to reject H₀. A shortfall of 2 g is within sampling error for n = 10.
Confidence interval: 248 ± 2.262 × 1.8974 = 248 ± 4.2920, giving (243.71 g, 252.29 g). The claimed 250 g lies inside it, agreeing with the test.
examples.answer: t = −1.0541 with df = 9, smaller in size than 1.833, so we fail to reject H₀; the 95% confidence interval is (243.71 g, 252.29 g).
examples.check:
import math
n = 10
xbar = 248.0
s = 6.0
mu0 = 250.0
se = s / math.sqrt(n)
t = (xbar - mu0) / se
t_crit = 1.833
t_ci = 2.262
half = t_ci * se
print(round(se, 4))
print(round(t, 4))
print(n - 1)
print(t_crit)
print(round(xbar - half, 4))
print(round(xbar + half, 4))

examples.question: A clinic records the fall in systolic blood pressure (in mmHg) for 6 patients after a drug: 4, 6, 3, 5, 7, 5. Test at α = 0.05 whether the drug lowers blood pressure on average. Use t(0.05, 5) = 2.015.
steps: Each patient gives one difference d, so this is a paired test. H₀: μ_d = 0. H₁: μ_d > 0. df = 5.
8.6603 > 2.015, so reject H₀. The mean fall is significantly greater than zero.
examples.answer: t = 8.6603 with df = 5, which exceeds 2.015, so we reject H₀: the drug lowers systolic pressure by a mean of 5.0000 mmHg.
examples.check:
import math
d = [4, 6, 3, 5, 7, 5]
n = len(d)
dbar = sum(d) / n
sd = math.sqrt(sum((x - dbar) ** 2 for x in d) / (n - 1))
se = sd / math.sqrt(n)
t = dbar / se
print(round(dbar, 4))
print(round(sd, 4))
print(round(se, 4))
print(round(t, 4))
print(n - 1)

traps: Degrees of freedom slip: n − 1 for one sample and paired data, but n₁ + n₂ − 2 for pooled two-sample. Writing n₁ + n₂ − 1 is the classic error.
Using 1.96 when n is small. The t critical value is larger, so 1.96 rejects too often and inflates the type I error.
Losing the sign. For one-tailed compare the signed t with the one-tailed critical value; for two-tailed compare |t| with t(α/2, df). Read direction from the sign of t before writing the conclusion.
Treating paired data as two independent samples. Difference the pairs first; ignoring pairing inflates the standard error and can hide a real effect.
Confusing pooled variance with a plain average. The pooled value weights each variance by n₁ − 1 and n₂ − 1, so a small group cannot swing it much, but a very small group makes s_p² unreliable.

quiz.q: Write the one-sample t statistic and give its degrees of freedom, defining every symbol.
quiz.a: t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n), df = n − 1, where x̄ is the sample mean, μ₀ the claimed mean, s the sample standard deviation with divisor n − 1, and n the sample size.

quiz.q: Why does the t distribution have heavier tails than the normal distribution?
quiz.a: σ is replaced by s, estimated from the same small sample and often too small. Dividing by a small standard error inflates the ratio, so extremes occur more often. Heavier tails keep the type I error at α.

quiz.q: A sample of 16 bulbs has mean life 52 hours and sample standard deviation 8 hours. Test at α = 0.05, two-tailed, whether the population mean is 48 hours. Use t(0.025, 15) = 2.131.
quiz.a: SE = 8/√16 = 2 hours. t = (52 − 48)/2 = 2.000, df = 15. |2.000| < 2.131, so fail to reject H₀; a gap of 4 hours is not significant at this sample size.

quiz.q: Group 1: n₁ = 8, x̄₁ = 30, s₁ = 4. Group 2: n₂ = 10, x̄₂ = 26, s₂ = 5. Test H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ at α = 0.05 using the pooled t-test with t(0.025, 16) = 2.120.

Two designs study the same drug: (a) 20 patients measured before and after, (b) 20 patients on drug compared with 20 different patients on placebo. Which gives the smaller standard error of the effect, and why?
quiz.a: Design (a). Pairing removes patient-to-patient variation, so the standard error of d̄ depends only on the spread of differences, usually much smaller than the spread between patients. Design (b) carries full between-patient variance into s_p, so its standard error is larger and its power lower for the same number of measurements.

quiz.q: A student reports t = 1.90 with df = 8 as significant at α = 0.05 two-tailed because 1.90 < 1.96. What is wrong, and what should the conclusion be?
quiz.a: The student used the normal critical value. With df = 8 the correct value is t(0.025, 8) = 2.306, which is larger. Since 1.90 < 2.306 the result is not significant; fail to reject H₀ and report a p-value or confidence interval to show the strength of evidence.

quiz.q: Give the confidence interval formula for a mean when σ is unknown.
quiz.a: x̄ ± t(α/2, n−1) × s/√n, where t(α/2, n−1) is the two-tailed critical value with n − 1 degrees of freedom and s/√n is the estimated standard error.

beyond: Not for the exam. The t-test is fairly robust to mild departures from normality, and most software reports it alongside the Welch version by default. When samples are tiny or clearly skewed, exact and permutation tests replace it. In industrial quality control the same formula reappears as the one-sample t chart for process monitoring. Search next for Welch's t-test, robustness of the t-test, and permutation tests for two samples.
